● High Vale now has a flat meadow landing, a spruce forest, moving clouds and a
  smoother join to the far mountains. It all runs at 33–39 ms per frame (roughly
  26–30 fps) on your laptop. I haven't done the boulders yet. The work is
  committed to wilderwake as b73122f, without your .ai/HANDOFF.md edit.

  - Meadow landing: the ground at the overlook is now a wide, gently sloping
    shelf instead of a 20% slope. The camera, grass and ground all use the same
    terrain data, so they stay in agreement.
  - Forest: about 50,000 spruce trees below the treeline, within 2.5 km of the
    overlook. They sway a little in the wind, and the treeline is ragged so a
    few trees climb higher. Further out the forest is painted onto the ground in
    the same patches, so there's no visible line where the real trees stop.
    - The overlook itself sits just above the treeline and looks down a long
      valley, so from the main viewpoint you mostly see the forest as dark
      slopes under the snowy peaks. Individual trees show up when you face the
      side ridges.
  - Clouds: moving clouds, lit warm near the sun and grey in their thick parts,
    fading into the haze at the horizon. My first version cost 5–10 ms per
    frame; after tuning, they add nothing measurable.
  - Seam: the far mountains used to drop 60 m in one hard step, which left a
    jagged band through the valley. That's now a smooth blend. The dark band
    still visible under the right-hand peaks is the forest line on mountains 8+
    km away, and it's now softer.

  Frame time is 3–5 ms slower than before because of the trees. If it feels
  sluggish, I can shrink the area with real trees from 2.5 km to 1.8 km.

  Up next: boulders in the meadow, and denser meadow grass (there's still bare
  ground between the clumps). Bishop Autopilot is still off, which the project's
  own rules also ask for.

● The grass is now longer and thicker, the meadow has boulders, and the ground
  has real texture. The catch is speed: it now runs at about 41–43 ms per frame
  (roughly 24 fps), down from 33–39 ms. The work is committed to wilderwake as
  1e7f175; I left your .ai/HANDOFF.md edit out.

  - Grass: blades are about 70% taller and wider, the close-in layer is denser,
    and the outer layer reaches 70 m. It now reads as a thick meadow right down
    to your feet, and it still moves in the wind.
  - Boulders: about 700 granite boulders in loose clusters, partly sunk into the
    turf, with lichen on top and moss at the base. Each has flat broken faces,
    so they look like cracked rock, not smooth blobs.
  - Ground texture: close up, the ground now has turf tussocks, dead-grass
    fibres, bare soil patches with pebbles, and scattered stones. Steep rock
    faces get layered bands and cracks, and the surface has small bumps that
    catch the light. It fades out by 260 m, where it would just blur anyway.

  Frame rate: almost all of the extra time is the grass. Lowering the render
  resolution barely helped (41 ms at 0.67), because the cost is the number of
  blades, not pixels. If 24 fps feels too choppy, I can dial the grass back a
  notch.

  For even more realism: the ground texture is generated in code. Real
  photo-scanned ground and rock textures would look better. ambientCG offers
  these free (CC0). It would be about 4–6 texture sets (grass, soil, rock),
  roughly 20–40 MB at 1K resolution. That's a download, so I need your go-ahead
  first.

  Screenshots are in wilderwake/shots/godot-*.png; godot-croft.png shows the
  boulders best.

● Yes, and the best route is to start from a real scanned tree. That means a
  large download, so I need your OK first.

  The asset: Fir Tree 01 on Poly Haven. It's free for any use (CC0 licence) and
  is built from photos of real fir trees: bark, layered needles, drooping
  branches. There's also Pine Tree 01, but it's twice the size and fir fits an
  alpine valley better.
  - File: fir_tree_01 glTF at 1K textures, from polyhaven.com.
  - Size: about 490 MB.

  The catch: the model has 7.8 million polygons, and your laptop can't draw
  50,000 of those. The file is only raw material for this plan:
  1. Build a lighter version in Blender (already on the machine, runs without
     opening a window). I'd photograph the scanned tree from 8–16 angles into a
     small texture sheet, capturing its colour and surface detail. From any
     distance past ~30 m, each tree then looks like the scanned one but costs
     about the same as the flat cards it has now.
  2. Close-up trees (a few hundred within ~150 m of the camera) get a
     much-reduced 3D version with real branches and the scanned bark and needle
     textures.
  3. Lighting and wind: the trees would get the sunlight glowing through needles
     and gentle sway, matching the grass.

  This should hold roughly today's frame time, maybe 2–4 ms more.

  No-download alternative: I build better trees entirely in code, with a proper
  trunk, drooping branch layers and a generated needle texture. It's a clear
  step up from now, but it won't reach "ultra realistic".

  Should I download Fir Tree 01 (~490 MB) and go with the scanned-tree plan?

❯ should I just generate low poly from tripo trees and other assets?            

● For trees, no. For other assets, often yes. It depends on what the asset is.

  Trees: stick with the scanned firs. Tripo makes one solid mesh, so foliage
  comes out as a lumpy shell. You can't see sky through the branches, the edges
  don't look like needles, and it can't sway in the wind. From a distance a
  Tripo tree reads as a green blob. That's the look you just moved away from.
  The scan-based trees we have now will look better than anything Tripo produces
  for trees.

  Where Tripo is a good fit:
  - Crafted props and buildings: the croft, stone walls, fences, carts, barrels,
    a shrine, bridges, signposts. These are solid objects with clear shapes,
    which is what it's good at.
  - Hero rocks: a few large, distinctive boulders or outcrops near the overlook,
    where you want a unique shape rather than a generated one.
  - Characters and creatures: as a starting point only. They still need proper
    rigging and cleanup.

  Where free scanned assets are better:
  - Ground and rock textures (the ambientCG option I mentioned earlier).
  - Scattered rocks and stones: Poly Haven has scanned rock models that beat
    both Tripo and my code-generated boulders.
  - More tree types, if you want variety beyond the firs, done the same way as
    the firs.

  How I'd use Tripo if you go ahead: generate the model, then run it through
  Blender automatically to cut the polygon count, fix its scale, check its
  textures, and export it for Godot. Its budget is capped at 20 generations a
  day, so I'd spend them on the few objects the player sees up close, like the
  croft and a couple of landmark rocks, not on anything repeated thousands of
  times.

  If you tell me which props High Vale needs first, I'll set up that Tripo →
  Blender → Godot pipeline and start with one.

  photos. Want me to do all three?

  firs, and they don't slow the game down at the overlook. I've sent three
  images: a crown up close, the same tree from about 15–25 m, and one of the

  5d2541e and e9a1786; your .ai/HANDOFF.md edit is still left out.

  - Trunk and branches: the scanned wood with its real bark textures, cut down
    to 5–9k triangles per tree.
  - Foliage: 500–1,800 small panels per tree, each placed where a cluster of the
    scan's needles actually is and angled along its branch. They show Blender
    renders of the scan's own branch tips. Each panel has per-needle lighting
    detail, so needles catch the sun individually and inner branches sit in
    shadow.

    version swap pixel by pixel, so there's no visible pop. Both sway in the
    wind.

  How it looks: up close the crown now reads as dense, layered conifer foliage
  with depth. My first two attempts looked like painted blobs, so I added
  per-needle lighting and twice as many smaller panels. It's a clear step up,
  but not photoreal: at 10–20 m it still looks a little painterly, because the
  needles are thinner than a pixel at game resolution.

  Frame rate: from the overlook the nearest tree is ~270 m away, so no 3D trees
  are drawn there. I ran old and new versions in alternating pairs, and they
  matched within noise every time. The absolute times were high (50–70 ms) for
  both, because the laptop was still hot from about an hour of Blender baking.

  valley grass shows unnatural banding from far away—both stemming from the

● User approved Claude's plan
  ⎿  Plan saved to: ~\.claude\plans\linear-waddling-clover.md · /plan to edit
     High Vale v2 — a small, beautiful, realistic basin you can walk

     Context

     Playtest feedback on the Godot High Vale:
     - The grass and trees look artificial, and the grass rustle sounds metallic
       (it's synthesized).
     - The world is far too big: it took about 5 minutes to walk to the trees.
     - Lucian floats on slopes.
     - His run looks "like a 2010 AI robot".
     - Overall it reads as "Ocarina of Time 1997", not realistic.

     The user wants High Vale much smaller and built around the canonical image
     creative/FEVER_CANONICAL_REFERENCE_LIBRARY/originals/regions/REG_01_HIGH_VA
     LE_REF_01.png: a ruined stone overlook, a forest and cliff band with
     waterfalls, and a castle on a lake.

     The machine has an Intel UHD with 1 GB, so realism has to come from
     photoscanned assets, lighting and composition, not raw GPU power.

     User decisions:
     - A playable area about 600 m across.
     - The castle kitbashed from the Tripo pieces already downloaded, plus a few
       new Tripo generations within tools/tripo_budget.json (that file is not
       edited).
     - Real CC0 audio may be downloaded; I show sources and sizes first.
     - For the run: fix the mocap retarget and hand-key polish on top, plus
       spring physics for the coat and hair.

     Approach (in order; each step is verified with captures before the next)

     1. A hand-authored hero basin, about 600 m (replaces "walk the 16 km DEM")

     - New godot/scripts/basin.gd plus a baked height field of about 700×700 m
       at 0.5 m per sample, generated by a script (tools/basin/build_basin.mjs)
       and laid over the existing DEM, which stays the mountain backdrop.
       - The layout follows the reference image: overlook ruins shelf (spawn) →
         sloping meadow → forest band at 60–150 m → cliff lip with two
         waterfalls dropping about 40 m and 25 m → river → lake with a castle
         promontory at about 300–400 m.
       - Sculpted with noise and splines, with explicit carving for the cliffs,
         river bed, lake bowl and paths.
     - Reuse terrain.gd's field/tile/LOD pipeline (field_texture, build_mesh,
       _cached, pads), pointing a new data/basin.bin at it. Grass (grass.gd,
       field uniform), trees (forest.gd) and height_at all read the same field
       unchanged.
     - Hard play bounds: a soft invisible wall plus the cliffs and lake. The DEM
       ground inside the basin is sunk under it with the existing
       sink_inside/sink_ramp.
     - Walk speed 1.1 → 1.4 m/s. Every landmark is within about 20–90 s of
       running.

     2. Lucian: grounded feet and a clean run

     - Foot planting in player.gd:
       - Body height is the lower of the two foot ground heights, smoothed, so
         he never floats.
       - A TwoBoneIK3D modifier per leg (present in Godot 4.7.2) lifts each foot
         onto the ground, with ankle alignment to the slope normal.
     - Run:
       - Try Run.fbx, Fast Run.fbx and Running.fbx through
         tools/blender/lucian_rig.py.
       - Fix the retarget's arm problem: align the upper-arm and forearm roll
         using the arm plane, not only bone direction, and scale the swing.
       - Then hand-key a correction layer in Blender:
         - forward torso lean of about 8–10°
         - relaxed hands
         - elbow at about 90°
         - arm arcs crossing the midline less
         - a vertical bob with head stabilisation
         - a slight pelvis rotation
       - Export as run, keeping speed matching.
     - Walk to run blend: a 1D blend space (AnimationTree) instead of a hard
       switch. Add start and stop.
     - SpringBoneSimulator3D on the coat tails and hair, if the Tripo mesh has
       usable weights. Otherwise bake spring motion in Blender.

     3. Real sound (CC0 downloads, listed with size before each lands)

     - Sounds to fetch:
       - grass rustle loops
       - footsteps on grass, soil and stone (6–10 variations each)
       - wind
       - waterfall roar (near and far layers)
       - lake lapping
       - birds
     - Sources: Poly Haven has no audio, so OpenGameArt CC0 and Pixabay's free
       licence (no login). Each file's licence and URL is recorded in
       godot/assets/audio/SOURCES.md.
     - ambience.gd:
       - 3D emitters at the waterfalls (roar gets louder as you approach, with
         low-pass by distance) and lapping at the lakeshore.
       - Footstep surface picked from the ground material under the foot.
     - Keep the synthesized music. The user didn't complain about it; its volume
       stays adjustable.

     4. Realistic vegetation (Poly Haven CC0 scans via existing 
     tools/ph_model.mjs)

     - Downloads (1K textures, decimated by the existing pipeline):
       grass_medium_01, grass_medium_02, fern_02, dandelion_01, nettle_plant,
       shrub_01–04, rock_moss_set_01/02, rock_face_01/02, tree_stump_01,
       dead_tree_trunk, moss_01. Exact sizes are shown before downloading.
     - Grass:
       - Replace the flat procedural blades in the near layer with clumps made
         from the scanned grass (alpha cards with real grass photos and
         normals), placed by the existing GPU scatter in
         grass.gdshader/grass.gd.
       - The far layer gets a baked impostor of the same clumps, and the ground
         shader's grass colours are resampled from the scan.
     - Trees:
       - Denser clustered forest bands, not scattered singles.
       - Near trees stay as real 3D scanned firs (fir_near), with more clusters
         per tree and a better crown AO bake.
       - Add pine_tree_01 as a second species via the same
         fir_impostor.py/fir_near.py pipeline, generalised to take an asset
         name.
     - Undergrowth (ferns, shrubs, stumps, mossy rocks) scattered by rules from
       the basin layout: forest floor, cliff base, path edges.

     5. Castle, waterfalls and lake

     - Castle:
       - Kitbash assets/converted/stone_gatehouse, stone_wall_pillar,
         mossy_stone_wall, stone_arch, stone_column and stone_house, decimated,
         with the Poly Haven castle_wall_slates material unified on top.
       - Add 2–4 Tripo generations (keep, round tower, curtain-wall segment,
         bridge) via tools/tripo.mjs --faces within the cap. --dry cost is shown
         first.
       - Assembled in a Blender script (tools/blender/castle_build.py) into one
         LODed GLB and a far impostor.
     - Waterfalls:
       - Scrolling, layered water-sheet meshes on the carved cliff lips.
       - A foam/mist particle system at the base (GPUParticles3D, low count,
         soft).
       - The waterfall sound emitters from step 3.
     - Lake and river: a water shader (depth tint from the field, fresnel sky
       reflection, normal-map ripples, shore foam) that also sits inside the DEM
       backdrop lake.

     6. Realism pass (lighting and camera)

     - Lighting:
       - Shorter shadow distance with 2 splits for crisp near shadows.
       - SSAO at half resolution if under 3 ms, and cheap volumetric fog/god
         rays toward the sun if under 3 ms. Otherwise use a baked sky-occlusion
         term in the ground and grass shaders.
     - Camera: filmic colour grade matched to the reference (warm highlights,
       cooler shadows, lifted blacks), plus mild DOF.
     - Budget: capture frameMs after each feature and keep the scene around
       33–40 ms at 1600×900. The shrunken world (far fewer terrain tiles, trees
       and grass cells) should free budget.

     Critical files

     - New: godot/scripts/basin.gd, tools/basin/build_basin.mjs,
       godot/shaders/water.gdshader, godot/shaders/waterfall.gdshader,
       tools/blender/castle_build.py, godot/assets/audio/SOURCES.md
     - Changed: godot/scenes/high_vale.tscn,

     - Reused: terrain.gd field and tile pipeline, tools/ph_model.mjs,
       tools/tripo.mjs (spending cap), tools/godot-build.mjs,
       tools/bishop-capture-godot.mjs, the capture spec player.hold driving test
       in high_vale.gd

● High Vale now: grass cut from real photo-scanned plants, low golden sun behind
  it, warm haze. Same idea as your UE video.

  › [image] shots\godot-gold-meadow.png (2.1MB)
  › [image] shots\godot-gold-vista.png (2.2MB)

● High Vale now uses photographed grass and a golden-hour sun, much like your
  video. The catch is speed: the meadow runs at about 50–57 ms per frame
  (roughly 18 fps), which will feel choppy. Everything so far is committed to
  wilderwake; I've sent two screenshots.

  About the video: it gets its look mostly from three things:
  - Photographed grass: every clump in the meadow is now cut from Poly Haven's
    real grass photo-scans, so the blades, seed heads and dry straw are real
    photos. The grass now stands 0.3–1.25 m tall, lower than the chest-high
    meadow in the previous version.
  - A low golden sun behind the grass: the sun now sits low and in front of you,
    so the grass glows at its edges, with bloom around the sun.
  - Warm haze in the air: light scatters toward the sun, and mist sits in the
    valley.

  The video was made in Unreal Engine 5, whose best lighting needs a real
  graphics card, which your laptop doesn't have. So I'm recreating the same
  effects in Godot instead.

  Other fixes from your playtest:
  - Smaller world: High Vale is now a compact valley about 600 m across, built
    around the official High Vale concept image:
    - the overlook meadow where you start
    - forest bands
    - a cliff where a 38 m waterfall will go, with a river below
    - a smaller cliff for a 29 m side waterfall
    - a lake with the castle headland
    - a far rim where the lake spills over

    From the start, you can run to the cliff in under a minute and to the lake
    in about 1.5 minutes.
  - Lucian stands on slopes properly now. His knees bend so both feet touch the
    ground on any slope. I measured his ankle height in six spots from flat to
    steep ground, and it stays within 4 mm everywhere; before the fix it was off
    by 8 cm on a side slope.
  - The robotic run is gone. I tried all three run animations you gave me side
    by side. Your "Running" file was what made him lean back with stiff arms,
    and "Fast Run" is clean. I also hand-tuned it: a forward lean while running,
    and his head raised so he looks ahead instead of at the ground.
  - Real recorded sound: a waterfall that gets louder as you approach, rivers,
    forest, wind, and real footsteps that change between grass and stone. The
    metallic grass sound is gone. One of the recordings (the Yo Frankie! nature
    set) requires a credit line, which I've written into
    godot/assets/audio/SOURCES.md.

  Not done yet:
  - The waterfalls themselves: the cliffs are there, but the falling water isn't
    yet.
  - The castle.
  - Ferns, bushes and mossy rocks: I've downloaded 14 photo-scanned plants from
    Poly Haven (about 30 MB) but haven't placed them yet.
  - Frame rate: the grass is the main cost, so I'll look for savings there once
    the castle and waterfalls are in.

  I'll start on the waterfalls and castle next, unless you'd rather I fix the
  frame rate first.

✻ Churned for 30m 34s · done Friday 6:48 PM

❯ ddoes rynning a game of 3.js need gpu                                         

● Yes. Three.js draws through WebGL (or WebGPU), and both run on the GPU. But
  almost any GPU will do, including the integrated one in your laptop (Intel
  UHD).

  - Integrated graphics: works. It's slower than a dedicated card, so what
    matters is how much you draw at once (triangle count, shadows, grass
    density). The limits are about the same as your Godot game hits now.
  - No GPU at all: the browser falls back to software rendering on the CPU
    (Chrome's SwiftShader). It technically runs but is very slow, only really
    usable for automated tests or screenshots, not for playing.
  - The browser costs a bit extra: the same scene usually runs somewhat slower
    in three.js than in native Godot on the same laptop. The browser adds its
    own overhead, and the web lacks some rendering features Godot uses.

  So a three.js game runs on your laptop, but it won't free you from the
  graphics limits you're already working around.

✻ Cogitated for 29s · done Friday 6:50 PM

❯ is there any way to like use another perons gpu or som                        

● Yes, you can play on a stronger computer somewhere else and stream the picture
  to your laptop. The game runs on their GPU and your laptop just shows the
  video, a bit like Netflix. There are three main ways:

  1. A friend's PC, using Parsec (free).
     - They install Parsec and let you connect. You then see and control their
       desktop with little delay.
     - The game files have to be on their PC, and they have to leave it on while
       you use it.
  2. Rent a cloud gaming PC.
     - Shadow PC is a full Windows computer in a data centre that you connect
       to, for a monthly fee.
     - GeForce NOW doesn't work for this: it only runs games from stores like
       Steam, not your own project.
  3. Rent a raw cloud GPU by the hour.
     - Services like Vast.ai, RunPod or AWS rent GPU machines, often well under
       $1/hour for strong cards.
     - Setting it up is more technical. You'd stream it with Parsec or
       Moonlight/Sunshine.
     - It's also good for heavy one-off jobs like Blender renders or bakes.

  Two catches:
  - Distance matters. If the machine is far away, every input lags. From South
    Africa, European servers usually add about 150–200 ms, which feels sluggish
    for an action game. Look for a Cape Town or Johannesburg data centre, or use
    a friend's PC nearby. You'll also want a steady connection of about 20+
    Mbps.
  - It only helps you, not your players. Everyone who plays the game runs it on
    their own hardware. Streaming lets you see higher-quality graphics while
    developing. But if you want most people to be able to play, the game still
    has to run well on ordinary laptops like yours.

  If you want to try it, the Parsec-to-a-friend's-PC route is free and takes
  about 10 minutes to set up.

✻ Crunched for 32s · done Friday 6:51 PM

❯ so we can pay for a cloud gpu. and build the game on that                     

● Yes, that works. Here's how it would change things and what to decide first.

  What it gets you:
  - You'd play and test on a strong GPU, streamed to your laptop.
  - The graphics budget goes way up: denser grass, more real 3D trees instead of
    flat stand-ins, better shadows and lighting, and higher-resolution
    textures.
  - Heavy jobs like the animation bakes and renders finish much faster.
  - It even makes Unreal Engine 5 an option, since that's what the grass video
    you showed me used. Switching engines would be a big move, though. Godot can
    get a lot better on a proper GPU too.

  Two ways to set it up:
  1. Everything in the cloud. A Windows cloud PC with a GPU, with Godot,
     Blender, the project and Claude Code installed on it. You connect with
     Parsec or Moonlight and work there as if it were your PC. This is the
     simplest day to day.
  2. Keep the laptop as home base, use the cloud for heavy lifting. Code stays
     here and syncs through git. The cloud machine does the bakes and renders,
     and runs the game when you want to play at full quality. It costs less,
     because you only pay while it's switched on.

  The big decision: who is the game for?
  If you build it on a strong GPU, it ends up needing a strong GPU. That's fine
  if your players will have decent gaming PCs. If you want it to run on ordinary
  laptops too, we keep your laptop as the "minimum spec" test machine and add
  quality settings (low/high).

  Practical notes:
  - Pick a nearby data centre. Look for one in Cape Town or Johannesburg, or
    streaming will feel laggy. Check that the provider actually offers GPU
    machines in that region before paying.
  - Rough costs:
    - Rented GPU machines: from well under $1 to about $1.50 an hour, and
      Windows machines cost more than Linux.
    - A monthly cloud gaming PC like Shadow: roughly $30–50 a month.
    - Prices change, so check current rates.
  - You do the signup and payment. I can't create accounts or enter card
    details. Once you have a machine, I can help install Godot and Blender, move
    the project over, and keep the private keys (like the Tripo key) off it
    unless you copy them yourself.

  I'd go with option 2, keeping your laptop as the low-spec check. Want me to
  compare providers with a GPU region near you?

     High Vale: cooking, menus, swords with combos, and the Lord Wren boss fight

     Context

     The owner wants four things added to the playable High Vale glade (50 m,
     pond, samurai placeholder):
     - cooking with a cooking pot
     - menus
     - swords with sword combos
     - a boss fight, designed first

     The canon supports all four (story/FEVER_FULL_GAME_BIBLE_V1_1_VISUAL.md):
     - High Vale's loop is "exploration, climbing, combat, cooking … a creature
       boss".
     - Its central problem is "noble storehouses are locked while … survivors
       need food now".
     - Food matters before bosses, and recipes give short-term benefits. There
       is no hunger meter.
     - Combat is: light attack, committed heavy, guard, parry, evasive step,
       roll, stamina, posture and enemy tells. No guns.
     - The UI looks like a field journal.

     The boss ties the other three features together. Lord Wren is a canon High
     Vale boss: a looter in ceremonial plate, hoarding the stores' food.
     - The owner fights him with the swords.
     - The owner prepares for him by cooking.
     - Beating him opens the food crates for a final shared meal.

     The canon Act One flagship is the four-legged Crooked Guest. It needs its
     own creature rig and animation work, so it becomes the next boss after this
     one.

     The boss fight: Lord Wren, "the Heir of the Stores"

     Setting
     - Wren has dragged the storehouse crates, which carry his family seal, into
       the glade across the pond from the camp.
     - He has set a looted banquet table there with brass goblets.
     - He carries a kite shield painted with his crest and a formal longsword
       (the antique estoc).
     - Reference: the canon prompt BOS_21
       (creative/.../prompts/01_MISSING_OFFICIAL_BOSS_PROMPTS_V1.md). Its image
       is still missing.
     - Region reference: REG_01_HIGH_VALE_REF_01.png.

     Intro
     - Crossing into his clearing starts a short subtitled exchange:
       - Wren: "Those crates carry my family's seal."
       - Lucian: "People are starving below the pass."
       - Wren: "Then they should have been born Wrens."
     - Then the boss bar appears, titled LORD WREN.

     Phase 1, The Duel (100–60 % health). Shield up, measured.
     - Guarded advance. His shield blocks frontal light attacks: a clang,
       sparks, and your stamina drained. The answer is a heavy attack, circling
       to his sword side, or parrying.
     - Crest Hook (the canon attack clue). He drops his shoulder and plants his
       back foot, the shield edge glints, then he hooks the shield forward and
       shoves.
       - If it hits, you're knocked down and he follows with a downward stab.
       - If you dodge sideways, his flank is open for about 1 s.
     - Heir's Three. A three-hit longsword combo with a delayed third hit, which
       catches button-mashers. Every hit can be parried; parrying all three
       does large posture damage.
     - Lunge thrust from 5–6 m. Sidestep it.

     Phase 2, Broken Crest (60–25 %).
     - Your next heavy hit cracks his shield (the canon "broken banquet
       shield"). He hurls it at you as a projectile you must dodge.
     - He then fights two-handed: a faster four-hit combo and a jump slash.
     - If you keep your distance, he throws looted goblets. These interrupt
       eating.
     - He drives you toward the pond. In water you wade slowly, but he won't
       wade in wearing plate. That gives you a breather while he throws things.

     Phase 3, Last Heir (≤ 25 %).
     - He feints, and his combos gain a hit.
     - Once he breaks off and runs to the banquet table to drink from a flask,
       which heals him 15 %. That's the moment to punish him: the player learns
       to read him.

     End
     - A posture break at low health drops him to one knee.
     - Prompt: Spare (he yields and leaves) or Strike. Canon allows human bosses
       to surrender.
     - Either way:
       - he drops Wren's Longsword (a new sword)
       - the crates open (chest-open animation) and give potatoes, onions, bread
         and salt
       - you cook Survivors' Supper at the pot
       - end card: "The stores are open. Tonight the vale eats."
     - If you die, you get "You fell", then Retry from the camp with the meals
       you had when the fight began.

     Preparation matters. Cooked meals are what make the fight winnable on a
     first try: extra stamina for parries and dodges, and heals you carry.
     Eating takes 1.2 s and leaves you open, so it's a risk.

     Player swordplay (Reed Form on the samurai's katana)

     Controls

     ┌────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────┐
     │           Action           │        Mouse/keyboard        │  Gamepad   │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Light attack (3–4-hit      │ LMB                          │ RB         │
     │ chain; input buffered)     │                              │            │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Heavy attack (breaks       │ hold LMB 0.35 s, or F        │ Y          │
     │ shields and posture)       │                              │            │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Guard / parry              │ hold RMB to guard, tap it    │ LB         │
     │                            │ for a 200 ms parry window    │            │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Dodge step with brief      │ Space (Shift+Space rolls)    │ B          │
     │ invulnerability            │                              │            │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Lock-on                    │ MMB / Tab                    │ R3         │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Eat meal                   │ R                            │ D-pad up   │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Sheathe                    │ Z                            │ —          │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Interact                   │ E                            │ X          │
     │                            │                              │ (existing) │
     ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
     │ Menu                       │ Esc                          │ Start      │
     └────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────┘

     - Riposte: LMB during a parry opening or posture break does a critical
       stab.
     - Combos: L-L-L(-L), L-L then Heavy (finisher), Sprint+L (lunge), Dodge+L
       (rising cut), Heavy charge.
     - Stamina: 100. Light 12, heavy 25, dodge 20, blocked hit 15–30. Refills at
       30/s after 0.6 s.
     - Health: 100.
     - Timing: all timing runs on real time, not frame count, and windows are
       generous, because the laptop runs at about 12–16 fps today (see
       Settings).
     - Swords:
       - Katana (balanced; Poly Haven antique_katana_01)
       - Saber (fast and light, shorter reach; wooden_handle_saber), on a rack
         at camp (katana_stand_01)
       - Wren's Longsword (slow and heavy, long reach, big posture damage;
         antique_estoc), the boss reward
       - Each sword has its own damage, speed, reach and combo chain. You swap
         swords in the menu or at the rack.
     - Practice post at camp, to learn the combos on.

     Cooking

     - The camp is at the path's end near the spawn, about (386, 376):
       - stone_fire_pit with a flickering fire (particle flames, light flicker,
         crackle sound)
       - brass_pot_01 over the fire
       - a bowl, spoon and cutting board, a stool, and the sword rack
     - Ingredients
       - Trout from the pond: E now keeps a caught fish, which goes into your
         creel.
       - Wild sorrel (shrub_sorrel_01) and wild onion (yellow_onion), foraged in
         the glade with a short harvest animation.
       - After the fight, crate goods: potato, bread, salt.
     - The cooking menu is a journal page at the pot: the recipes, what each
       needs, and what it does. You cook by kneeling at the pot for about 3 s,
       with steam and bubbling. Recipes:
       - Grilled Trout (1 trout): a carried meal that heals 40.
       - Trout & Sorrel Stew (1 trout, 2 sorrel, 1 onion): for 5 minutes, +25
         max stamina and +30 % stamina regen.
       - Sorrel Broth (2 sorrel): a carried meal that heals 25 over 6 s.
       - Survivors' Supper (after Wren): the end beat.
     - Carried meals: up to 3 slots, eaten with R.

     Menus (journal style: parchment panels, Georgia serif via SystemFont, no 
     downloads)

     - Title: "FEVER — High Vale". Start, Settings, Quit.
     - Pause (Esc):
       - Resume
       - Journal: recipes, controls, and what you know about Wren
       - Equipment: choose a sword, see your meals
       - Settings, Retry fight, Quit
     - Settings:
       - Quality preset: Laptop or High, the High one for a cloud GPU. Laptop
         sets grass density, shadow distance and render scale.
       - Mouse sensitivity, invert Y, volume.
       - Saved to user://settings.cfg, guarded so the capture sandbox still
         runs.
     - Laptop preset target: at most 40 ms per frame in the arena. It's
       measured, and if it can't be met I'll report the number.
     - HUD (canon: minimal): health and stamina bottom-left, three meal slots,
       an interaction prompt, the boss bar and subtitles.

     Assets (all CC0; downloads need your go-ahead, which approving this plan 
     gives for this list)

     - Quaternius Universal Animation Library 2, Standard: itch.io, 17 MB. It
       has sword combos split into single hits with recoveries, knockback,
       shield idle, jump slash, overhand throw, harvest and chest open. It uses
       the same skeleton as the library the walk came from, so the retarget
       pipeline handles it directly.
     - Already on disk:
       - library 1: Roll, Hit_Chest/Hit_Head, Death01, Sword_Idle/Attack,
         Fixing_Kneeling (for cooking), Interact
       - Mixamo: Draw A Great Sword 2, Sheathing Sword
     - Poly Haven models (1k glTF), about 46 MB total:
       - antique_katana_01 0.6 MB, wooden_handle_saber 1.7, antique_estoc 2.4,
         kite_shield 3.6, katana_stand_01 0.5
       - stone_fire_pit 2.4, brass_pot_01 1.5
       - wooden_bowl_01 1.7, wooden_spoon 1.9, wooden_cutting_board 1.9,
         wooden_stool_01 0.9
       - wooden_crate_01 2.2, wooden_crate_02 2.1, treasure_chest 5.2,
         WoodenTable_01 0.5, brass_goblets 4.6
       - shrub_sorrel_01 1.1, yellow_onion 1.7, sweet_potato 1.7, hamburger_buns
         2.2 (bread), wicker_basket_01 2.6
       - dry_branches_medium_01 3.1
     - Sounds: sword swings, metal clashes, parries, hits, fire crackle, pot
       bubbling. Candidates are Kenney RPG Audio and Impact Sounds (CC0) and
       OpenGameArt CC0. I'll list each file and its size and ask before
       downloading them, as a separate confirmation.
     - Wren's body: a placeholder built from the samurai mesh, re-tinted to
       black-and-silver plate, 1.08× scale, with the kite shield and estoc. If
       you make a Lord Wren model in Tripo, as you did for the samurai, it drops
       into the same pipeline and replaces the placeholder.

     Implementation (milestones, each verified before the next)

     1. Animation pipeline (tools/blender/lucian_rig.py)
        - One-shot clips (name=ual2:Clip!once): the whole clip, no loop search.
        - A root-motion curve saved to JSON.
        - The hit window worked out automatically from blade-tip speed in the
          bake.
        - Leg IK on for all sources.
        - Bake the player set and Wren's set to godot/assets/samurai/ and
          godot/assets/wren/.
        - In lucian_join.py, split the modelled hip katana from the samurai mesh
          if it's a separate loose part, so it can hide while the sword is
          drawn. If it isn't separate, the blade in hand shows only while drawn.
     2. Game state and UI
        - scripts/game.gd autoload (registered in project.godot): health,
          stamina, inventory, meals, buffs, equipped sword, flags, pause.
        - scripts/hud.gd.
        - scripts/menu.gd: title, pause, journal, equipment, settings, cooking
          page.
        - Quality presets hook into grass.gd, undergrowth.gd, the Sun and the
          render scale.
     3. Camp and cooking
        - scripts/camp.gd: fire pit, fire shader and particles, light, pot,
          props, sword rack, practice post.
        - scripts/forage.gd: sorrel and onion pickups.
        - data/recipes.json.
        - pond.gd: a caught trout goes into the creel.
     4. Combat
        - scripts/player_combat.gd: the sword attached to hand_r
          (BoneAttachment3D), combo state machine, guard and parry, dodge,
          lock-on, stamina, eating, hit reactions, death.
        - player.gd switches from AnimationPlayer crossfades to an
          AnimationTree: locomotion, then an upper-body guard layer, then a
          one-shot action slot. Walk and run stay unchanged.
        - Hits: a swept blade segment tested against a capsule. Hit-stop, camera
          shake, sparks.
     5. Boss
        - scripts/enemy.gd (health, posture, hurt capsule, reactions) and
          scripts/lord_wren.gd (the phase state machine, attacks with wind-ups,
          shield blocking, projectiles, flask, spare/strike).
        - The arena and banquet camp across the pond.
          tools/glade/build_glade.mjs gains a flattened arena clearing, then the
          glade is rebuilt.
        - Intro and outro subtitles, crate rewards, Survivors' Supper, end card.

     Critical files

     - New: godot/scripts/{game,hud,menu,camp,forage,player_combat,enemy,lord_wr
       en}.gd, godot/data/recipes.json, godot/assets/{props,wren}/,
       godot/shaders/fire.gdshader.
     - Changed: godot/scripts/{player,pond,high_vale,grass,undergrowth}.gd,
       godot/project.godot (autoload), godot/scenes/high_vale.tscn,
       tools/blender/{lucian_rig,lucian_join}.py, tools/glade/build_glade.mjs.
     - Reused:
       - the lucian_rig.py retarget and leg IK
       - Obstacles.resolve (bodies and the arena edge)
       - terrain.height_at / mask_at (placement, water)
       - the pond's grab and HUD pattern (pond.gd:_make_hud, _label)
       - the capture harness in high_vale.gd (player.hold, burst)
       - the Blender cycle renders (scratch render_cycle.py) for reviewing clips

     Verification

     - node tools/godot-build.mjs is clean after each milestone.
     - Clips: contact sheets rendered in Blender, side and back views, for every
       combat clip. Hit windows are printed from the bake.
     - Capture harness (--bishop-capture with player.hold), scripted checks:
       - an L-L-L-H combo on the practice post prints hits and damage
       - a parry against a scripted Wren swing prints "parried" and posture
         damage
       - dodge invulnerability prints "no hit"
       - cook a stew and print the buff
       - eat a meal and print the heal
       - force Wren through each phase and print the phase changes
       - the victory flow opens the crates
     - Screenshots at the camp, the menus, mid-combo, parry sparks, each Wren
       phase, and the end card.
     - Frame time logged for the arena under both quality presets.
     - Commits at each milestone, never including .ai/HANDOFF.md. Then I
       relaunch the game for you to playtest.

     Deliberately out of scope

     - The Crooked Guest (next boss: creature rig).
     - Survivor NPC models. The survivors are only mentioned in dialogue.
     - Save/load beyond settings, climbing, and other weapon forms.
     - A final Lord Wren model and voice acting.

● The game is open with all four features in. It starts on a title screen; click
  Begin.

  The boss: Lord Wren

  He's a looter in black-and-silver plate who has dragged the storehouse food
  crates into the clearing across the pond. Walk toward his crates and he
  speaks, then the fight starts.

  1. Phase 1 (shield up): light hits bounce off his shield.
     - A heavy attack or a parry opens him up.
     - When his shield edge glints and he drops his shoulder, that's the Crest
       Hook. It can't be blocked, so roll sideways.
     - His three-cut chain has a late third hit.
  2. Phase 2 (below 60% health): your next heavy hit cracks the shield and he
     throws it at you. He then fights two-handed, jumps in with a slash, and
     throws goblets if you keep your distance. He won't follow you into the
     pond.
  3. Phase 3 (below 25%): he feints, and once runs to his table to drink from a
     flask. Hit him while he drinks.
  4. The end: beaten, he kneels. Press E to spare him, or strike. Either way he
     drops his longsword (a third sword for you) and his crates open. Cook the
     Survivors' Supper at your fire to finish.

  Cooking

  Your camp is at the end of the path, with a fire, a pot, a sword rack and a
  practice post.
  - Ingredients: catch trout in the pond (E, then E again to keep it). Pick
    sorrel in the meadow and wild onions at the forest edge.
  - At the pot (E): Grilled Trout heals 40. Trout & Sorrel Stew gives more
    stamina for 5 minutes, which is the one to eat before Wren. Sorrel Broth
    heals over time.
  - You can carry 3 meals and eat one with R. Eating takes a moment and leaves
    you open.

  Lord Wren model prompt

  Step 1: make a reference image first (Whisk or ChatGPT). Tripo builds much
  better models from a clean image than from text alone.

  Full-body character reference, front view, A-pose (arms held 30 degrees away 
  from the body, legs slightly apart), standing on a plain light-grey 
  background, even studio lighting, no shadows. Lord Wren: a ruthless nobleman 
  turned looter, late 40s, lean and hard-faced, sharp cheekbones, short 
  grey-streaked black hair swept back, trimmed beard, cold pale eyes, a thin 
  scar through one eyebrow, bare head. He wears battered ceremonial plate armour
  in blackened steel with polished silver edging, dented and scratched. A 
  family crest of a small wren bird is embossed in silver on the breastplate. 
  Mail at the elbows and knees, articulated gauntlets and sabatons, a short torn
  dark-crimson tabard hanging to mid-thigh, a wide leather belt with a silver 
  buckle. Empty hands, no weapon, no shield, no cape, no helmet. Realistic, 
  grounded, premium dark-fantasy game character, high detail, photoreal 
  materials. No fantasy crown, no glowing effects, no aura.

  Step 2: Tripo (image to model, from that picture).
  - If Tripo asks for a text prompt: realistic dark fantasy nobleman in battered
    black and silver plate armour, A-pose, empty hands, game character
  - Rig: use the same humanoid auto-rig you used for the samurai, so the bone
    names match my pipeline. Export as FBX.
  - Checks before you send it:
    - Empty hands. I attach his sword and shield separately.
    - No long cape or flowing cloth; they rig badly.
    - Arms clear of the body.
    - One solid body, not floating pieces.
  - Face and bare head are on purpose, so he can visibly talk later. If you want
    a helmet, make it a separate model and I'll attach it.

  What separates this from an AA boss fight

  1. The character
  - He's the samurai re-coloured; he needs his own model, as above.
  - Damage states: the shield physically shatters into pieces (right now it just
    disappears), armour dents and dirt build up by phase, and the tabard tears.
  - Face: a jaw and mouth that move when he speaks, and eyes and head that track
    you.
  - Cloth that moves (the tabard) instead of stiff armour.
  - The player is also still a stand-in (the samurai, not Lucian).

  2. Animation. This is the biggest gap.
  - Both fighters share one library sword set: 3 swings, 1 heavy, 1 lunge.
  - An AA boss has 60–150 of his own animations:
    - signature attacks per phase
    - circling and strafing: he can't circle you now, he only walks at you
    - stepping back, sidestepping and dodging
    - turning in place without his feet sliding
    - taunts
    - hit reactions by direction (front, back, left, right), plus heavy staggers
    - phase-change animations
    - kneeling, surrendering and death scenes
  - Blending: the upper and lower body animate separately (walk while guarding),
    hands grip the weapon properly, the head looks at you, and attacks stretch
    to reach your actual distance.
  - Player: no circling while locked on, no directional dodges (roll only), no
    walking guard, no real riposte animation (it reuses the heavy), no finishing
    move.

  3. Moveset and AI
  - Moveset: now 8 attacks picked by weighted chance. AA means 12–20 per phase:
    - branching combos: he changes the chain depending on where you are
    - delayed and feinted attacks
    - a grab
    - a sweeping area attack
    - gap-closers
    - anti-heal punishes: he rushes you when you eat
    - anti-spam answers: he punishes roll spam and hanging back
  - AI: it should read your state (attacking, healing, low stamina, keeping
    away), manage distance, learn your habits (the bible asks for this), with a
    defined aggression curve and difficulty levels.
  - Hit detection: per-attack hitboxes on specific frames, a hurtbox per body
    part, per-frame "can't be interrupted" windows, and directional knockback.
    Now it's a blade sweep with a generous fallback.
  - Execution: a proper riposte or finisher scene, slow motion on the final blow
    and on a perfect parry.

  4. Frame rate. Timing combat needs a steady 30–60 fps; this laptop gives
  15–23. Nothing else matters as much if parries feel random. Fix it with the
  cloud GPU or more optimisation (mainly the distant forest).

  5. Presentation and camera
  - Intro cutscene: camera shots of Wren at his stolen banquet, his name card, a
    music hit.
  - Short phase-change scenes: slow-motion shield shatter, a line of dialogue.
  - Ending scene: spare or strike, staged with camera work.
  - Camera: a lock-on camera that keeps both of you framed and never goes
    through trees, and a punch of field of view on heavy hits.
  - Effects: sword trails, dust on impacts, a shockwave on heavy landings, scuff
    marks on the ground, spilled wine from goblets and the flask, a shattering
    shield. Kept grounded, no magic auras (canon).

  6. Arena
  - Now it's a grassy clearing with crates and a table.
  - AA:
    - a built arena: the canon ruined banquet under a collapsed arch
    - survivors kept at a distance, reacting to the fight
    - breakable crates and a table he kicks over
    - a banner with his crest
    - lighting that keeps the fight readable (the fights I filmed were dark and
      muddy)

  7. Sound. Right now there is none.
  - Sound effects:
    - swings per weapon
    - metal-on-metal clashes, a distinct parry ring, shield hits
    - armour clanking with every step
    - cloth and leather movement
    - effort grunts and breathing for both fighters
    - body falls
    - shield shatter, goblets clattering, flask drinking
    - fire and pot for the camp
  - Music: a boss theme built in layers: intro, a loop, and more intensity for
    phases 2 and 3. Plus short cues for phase change, a parry, and victory, and
    quiet beats before key moments. The music drops when he speaks.

  8. Voice. He needs real spoken lines, not only subtitles:
  - the intro exchange
  - taunts: when you heal, after a parry, when you die
  - lines at each phase change
  - grunts when hurt
  - surrender and last words
  - his mouth moving to the words
  - Lucian's lines too

  9. Story around the fight
  - Now the setup is one paragraph of text.
  - AA:
    - survivors you meet before the fight
    - a reason to prepare (someone tells you about his shield)
    - notes on Wren's past (the grandfather's shield)
    - a Supper scene where you see the people eat, not just an end card

  10. HUD and flow
  - phase ticks on his health bar
  - a stagger indicator
  - a fast retry next to the arena instead of back at camp
  - a first-time parry prompt
  - difficulty options (the bible's accessibility list)
  - a checkpoint save

  11. Testing. Everything is script-tested only; you're the first person to
  fight him. AA means rounds of playtesting and tuning.

  What I need from you before we start

  1. The model (above).
  2. Sound effects: OK to download the four free packs I listed (about 14.5 MB)?
     I'll also look for more armour and foley sounds and ask the same way.
  3. Music: free licensed tracks (fine, but generic), an AI-made track (a paid
     service on your account), or a composer?
  4. Voice:
     - free Windows text-to-speech: robotic, I wouldn't
     - an AI voice service: good quality, paid, needs your account and key
     - a person recording the lines: best quality
  5. Animations: the big jump needs more clips. Mixamo is free, but it needs
     your Adobe login, so you'd download the "Sword and Shield Pack" and "Great
     Sword Pack". Together they're roughly 100 clips, including circling,
     directional hits, dodges, turns and blocks.
